Fourier analysis

 Home Mathematics Area of mathematics Analysis
OurBigBook.com Words: 14k Articles: 190
Fourier analysis describes a function by the oscillations that compose it. A graph records values at successive positions or times; a frequency spectrum records how much of each frequency is present, together with its wave phase. The same complicated shape can become a short list of simple components. For periodic functions, the components form a Fourier series; on the whole real line, the Fourier transform uses a continuous range of frequencies, and the Fourier inversion theorem puts them back together.
For a concrete example, consider the trigonometric polynomial
f(t)=cos(2πt)+21​cos(6πt)+41​cos(10πt).
(1)
With t measured in seconds, its three Fourier harmonics have frequencies 1, 3, and 5 cycles per second and amplitudes 1, 1/2, and 1/4. Each cosine has zero wave phase. Adding them creates the sharper peaks in the figure. The frequency spectrum makes the recipe immediately visible; changing an amplitude changes the shape without changing the component's frequency. Fourier orthogonality lets us recover each Fourier coefficient by averaging against the corresponding sine or cosine, because the other Fourier harmonics cancel over a full period of a function.
The deeper reason these components are so useful is that they simplify operations. By Euler's formula, the exponential function eiωx packages a cosine and a sine into one Fourier mode. A translation or a derivative changes only its multiplier:
eiω(x−a)=e−iωaeiωx,dxd​eiωx=iωeiωx.
(2)
Thus Fourier modes are simultaneous eigenfunctions of these operations. In Fourier series, this gives a literal diagonalization in the Fourier basis; on the real line, the Fourier transform gives the continuous counterpart, with each frequency handled separately. The Translation property of the Fourier transform and the Fourier transform of a derivative turn shifting and differentiating a whole function into multiplication of its Fourier transform. A convolution likewise becomes multiplication by the convolution theorem. This is beautiful because one description simplifies several apparently different operations at once.
For example, the heat equation ut​=κuxx​, with thermal diffusivity κ>0, evolves a spatial Fourier mode as
u(x,t)=Ae−κω2teiωx.
(3)
Fine ripples have larger angular frequencies and decay faster: the formula explains why heating smooths a jagged temperature profile. For a general initial profile with sufficient regularity, the Fourier transform gives u(ω,t)=e−κω2tu(ω,0), and Fourier inversion recovers the temperature. Similarly, multiplying selected parts of a frequency spectrum suppresses unwanted components. Claude E. Shannon's Communication in the Presence of Noise (1949), Section III, describes ideal filtering as a projection that retains some frequency coordinates and removes others.[ref]
The physical motivation is already visible in Joseph Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur (1822). Chapter III constructs heat profiles using sums of sines and cosines; Chapter IX, articles 355–359, passes from Fourier series to integrals as the spatial interval becomes unbounded. These heat problems explain the motivation for the discrete and continuous descriptions. Their modern formulations specify which functions admit reconstruction and in what sense the expansions converge.[ref][ref]

Infrared cutoff (qmin​)

Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
A lower included wavenumber. A finite periodic patch of size L has smallest nonzero wavenumber of order 2π/L; supports and boundary conditions can change the factor. The cutoff limits large-scale fluctuations.

Words: 29
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
Fourier shell correlation compares two three-dimensional maps using their complex Fourier transform coefficients in successive reciprocal-space shells. Independent half-map refinement helps distinguish reproducible signal from overfitting; masking and correlated inputs can bias the result.

Cross-correlation ((f⋆g)(x)=∫R​f(y)​g(x+y)dy)

Words: 185 Articles: 2
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
For this sign convention, cross-correlation compares a function with translated copies of another, conjugating the first factor. If f,g∈L1(R), Fubini's theorem gives Fourier transform f⋆g​(k)=f​(k)​g​(k). Indeed, the substitution s=x+y factors the double integral into ∫f(y)​eikydy and ∫g(s)e−iksds. The zero-lag value for f=g∈L2 is the squared L2 norm. Fourier inversion applied to this correlation proves the Parseval identity, first for Schwartz functions and then by density for L2 space.

Correlator

Words: 46
Cross-correlation OurBigBook.com
A device or algorithm that estimates the cross-correlation of input signals, often by multiplying one signal by a delayed or complex-conjugated copy of another and averaging. In radio interferometry, calibrated complex correlations supply complex visibilities. Delay tracking, channel width and integration duration determine which field information survives that averaging.

Autocorrelation of a square-integrable function (h(x)=∫R​f(y)​f(y+x)dy)

Words: 72
Cross-correlation OurBigBook.com
This deterministic, unnormalized cross-correlation of a function with itself exists for every shift when f∈L2, by the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality. It satisfies h(0)=∥f∥22​ and h(−x)=h(x)​. With Fourier transform convention f​(k)=∫e−ikxf(x)dx, its transform is ∣f​∣2, in the tempered distribution sense when the correlation is not integrable. Fourier inversion at zero gives the Parseval identity, first for Schwartz functions and then by approximation in L2 space. Unlike the normalized statistical autocorrelation, its value at zero is not generally one.

Wiener-Khinchin theorem (Γ(τ)=∫S(Ω)e−iΩτdΩ)

Words: 55
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
The Wiener-Khinchin theorem relates the autocorrelation of a weakly stationary process to its power spectral density by a Fourier transform. The displayed convention is appropriate when the optical correlation is Γ(τ)=⟨f∗(t)f(t+τ)⟩ and the analytic field contains e−iωt. A Lorentzian line shape of half-width κ gives exponential correlation decay e−κ∣τ∣, including the carrier factor e−iωτ when the full field is correlated.

Frequency spectrum

Words: 98 Articles: 1
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
A frequency spectrum describes the frequency components of a function. A Fourier series supplies discrete Fourier coefficients; the Fourier transform of an integrable function supplies a continuous, generally complex-valued description. An amplitude plot shows magnitudes and omits wave phases, so it need not determine the original function. In the example with three Fourier harmonics above, the one-sided amplitude plot has heights 1, 1/2, and 1/4. The corresponding complex Fourier coefficients at positive and negative frequencies each have half those heights: cos(2πνt)=(e2πiνt+e−2πiνt)/2.

Spectrogram

Words: 26
Frequency spectrum OurBigBook.com
A spectrogram displays how a local frequency spectrum changes over time, usually using colour for squared Fourier transform magnitude. Longer analysis windows give finer frequency spacing while averaging over a longer time interval.

Spatial frequency (ν=1/Λ)

Words: 39
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
Spatial frequency is the number of oscillation cycles per unit length. A ripple with spatial period Λ has frequency ν=1/Λ; its angular wavenumber is k=2πν. In two dimensions the spatial-frequency vector specifies the orientation and period of a plane-wave pattern.

Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem (fs​≥2B,T=1/fs​)

Words: 892 Articles: 6
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem says that a bandlimited function can be recovered exactly from equally spaced samples, provided the sampling rate is high enough. It is the bridge between a continuous waveform and a sequence of numbers: the missing values between samples are determined by the restriction on its frequencies.
Here is a precise finite-energy version. Let f∈L2(R), meaning ∫R​∣f(t)∣2dt<∞, and suppose its Fourier transform, defined through the Plancherel theorem, is zero outside [−2πB,2πB]. Thus B>0 is the largest allowed ordinary frequency, in cycles per second, rather than an angular frequency. Set T=1/fs​, where fs​ is the number of samples per second. If fs​≥2B, the continuous representative of f is recovered by
f(t)=∑n∈Z​f(nT)π(t/T−n)sin(π(t/T−n))​.
(4)
The quotient is the normalized sinc function, with value one when its argument is zero. Each shifted sinc function is one at its own sampling time and zero at every other sampling time. Its coefficient is therefore exactly the required sample value. For this L2 space formulation, the reconstruction converges in the L2 space norm and uniformly in t. The critical rate fs​=2B is allowed for this class; choosing fs​>2B leaves a gap between the occupied frequencies and the sampling boundary.
For a numerical example, a bandlimited function with no frequencies above 3 cycles per second can be reconstructed from its samples every 0.1 seconds: fs​=10>6. Exact reconstruction uses the whole sequence indexed by Z. A finite recording and a finite sum of sinc functions introduce truncation error; joining adjacent samples by straight lines is generally a different reconstruction.
The obstruction is aliasing. At sampling rate fs​=10, the two distinct waveforms
f2​(t)=cos(2π⋅2t),f8​(t)=cos(2π⋅8t)
(5)
have identical samples at t=n/10, because
cos(2π⋅8n/10)=cos(2πn−2π⋅2n/10)=cos(2π⋅2n/10).
(6)
The samples alone cannot tell whether the waveform oscillates twice or eight times per second. If we know in advance that all frequencies are below 5, the 8-cycle waveform is excluded and the ambiguity disappears. These pure cosines are an illustrative aliasing example, rather than members of the finite-energy L2 space class in the stated theorem.
Exactly at a sampling boundary, the function class matters. At rate fs​, the sine sin(2π(fs​/2)t) has zero values at every n/fs​. It is a nonzero waveform indistinguishable from zero on that grid, but has infinite energy and is excluded by the finite-energy hypothesis above. This explains why a rule intended to cover arbitrary pure sinusoids should demand a strict inequality. For spatial data, replace seconds by distance: the Nyquist spatial frequency is 1/(2p) for sample pitch p.
The proof idea is short: the samples are Fourier coefficients of the Fourier transform restricted to a sampling-sized frequency interval. Because a bandlimited function has no contribution outside that interval, its Fourier series determines the whole Fourier transform; Fourier inversion then gives the sinc function expansion. See sampling expansion by periodic Fourier projection for this connection.
Claude E. Shannon's Communication in the Presence of Noise (1949), Section II, Theorem 1 and equation (7), gives the sampling statement and reconstruction using shifted sinc functions in a communication setting. Shannon explicitly notes earlier mathematical forms and credits Nyquist with emphasizing the sampling interval in telegraphy.[ref]

Nyquist frequency (fs​/2)

Words: 31
Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem OurBigBook.com
For uniform samples at rate fs​, the frequency fs​/2 is the Nyquist frequency. A real baseband signal confined below this boundary can avoid spectral overlap when an appropriate anti-aliasing filter is used.

Aliasing (e2πi(ν+mfs​)n/fs​=e2πiνn/fs​,m,n∈Z)

Words: 153 Articles: 1
Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem OurBigBook.com
Aliasing is the inability to distinguish different continuous frequencies from sampled values. The identity above says that frequencies separated by an integer multiple of the sampling rate fs​ give identical samples of a complex Fourier mode. For real cosines, changing the sign of a frequency also gives the same waveform, explaining the 2-versus-8 example at rate 10. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem prevents this ambiguity within its specified class of bandlimited functions. Before sampling, unwanted higher frequencies must be suppressed if they would violate that assumption; once two waveforms give the same samples, those samples cannot identify which was present.

Anti-aliasing filter

Words: 61
Aliasing OurBigBook.com
An anti-aliasing filter suppresses signal components outside the intended acquisition band before sampling. For voltage recording it is an analogue filter ahead of the analog-to-digital converter, with a transition band allowed below half the sampling rate. Once two frequencies have become indistinguishable through aliasing, a digital filter generally cannot recover the lost distinction. The Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem concerns an already bandlimited function; a physical filter approximates that prerequisite.

Strictly supercritical sampling alias counterexample (g(t)=sin(πt)h(t),g(n)=0)

Words: 67
Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem OurBigBook.com
For every ϵ>0, choose a nonzero smooth spectral bump supported in (−ϵ0​,ϵ0​) with ϵ0​<min(ϵ,π), and let h be its inverse Fourier transform. Then g is a nonzero Schwartz function, vanishes on all integer samples, and its transform is the difference of bumps shifted to π and −π. Its support lies strictly within [−π−ϵ,π+ϵ]. Thus even a small bandwidth increase destroys uniqueness from unit-spaced samples.

Sampling expansion by periodic Fourier projection (f(t)=∑n∈Z​f(n)π(t−n)sin(π(t−n))​)

Words: 82
Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem OurBigBook.com
When the continuous Fourier transform F of an integrable function vanishes outside [−π,π], its periodic Fourier coefficients are the integer samples of the continuous representative of f, with the sign of the index reversed. Projecting F in L2[−π,π] and then applying the Fourier inversion theorem gives the displayed reconstruction using the normalized sinc function, with each quotient defined as one when t=n. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality controls the reconstruction error uniformly in t. Bessel's inequality bounds the vector of shifted sinc functions, giving absolute uniform tails when the sample sequence belongs to ℓ2.

Nyquist spatial frequency (νmax​=1/(2p))

Words: 49
Nyquist–Shannon sampling theorem OurBigBook.com
Samples spaced by pitch p can distinguish spatial frequencies strictly below 1/(2p) cycles per unit length. Thus the shortest limiting wavelength is 2p; exactly at the limit a sinusoid's phase can make all samples vanish. A practical deformable mirror has additional limits from actuator influence functions and finite pupil geometry.

A Euclidean lattice is a discrete subgroup Λ⊆Rn spanning the ambient vector space. Its covolume m(Λ) is the volume of a fundamental parallelepiped.

Lenstra-Lenstra-Lovász lattice basis reduction algorithm (δ=3/4,∣μij​∣≤1/2)

Words: 104
Euclidean lattice OurBigBook.com
For an integer basis of a Euclidean lattice, the algorithm uses integer column operations and swaps to obtain a size-reduced basis with Gram-Schmidt coefficients ∣μij​∣≤1/2 and the condition δ∥bi∗​∥2≤∥bi+1∗​∥2+μi+1,i2​∥bi∗​∥2. It preserves the lattice and exposes short vectors and near-relations. It is useful for improving proven Diophantine bounds by encoding scaled logarithms in integer coordinates. A certified lower bound for every nonzero lattice vector is mini​∥bi∗​∥: in a nonzero integer linear combination, project onto the last nonzero Gram-Schmidt direction. Better-reduced bases improve this lower bound. Rounding and logarithm errors must still be bounded before turning it into a certified lower bound for a logarithmic form.

Complex lattice (Λ=Zω1​+Zω2​⊂C)

Words: 81 Articles: 1
Euclidean lattice OurBigBook.com
A complex lattice is a discrete rank-two subgroup of the complex plane, generated by two real-linearly independent periods. An oriented basis can be chosen with Im(ω1​/ω2​)>0. Scaling by ω2−1​ then gives Zτ+Z for a point in the complex upper half-plane.

Homothety of complex lattices (Λ′=aΛ, a∈C×)

Words: 40
Complex lattice OurBigBook.com
Two complex lattices are homothetic when multiplication by one nonzero complex number takes one onto the other. Changes between oriented integral bases have determinant one, so normalized period ratios classify these classes by SL2​(Z)\H. The lattice Eisenstein sums scale as Gk​(aΛ)=a−kGk​(Λ).

Tetracode length-isospectral lattice construction (L±​=(±3I+S)Z4)

Words: 293 Articles: 3
Euclidean lattice OurBigBook.com
For the skew matrix S=(0−1−1−1​101−1​1−101​11−10​), both Euclidean lattices reduce to the tetracode modulo 3. A reflection depending on the reduction coset matches their vectors coordinatewise in absolute value. Their weighted length spectra agree for all positive diagonal axis weights. Rationally independent weights force any possible linear isometry to be a coordinate sign change; the code then forces an overall sign, which does not identify the two lattices.

Rationally independent axis weights obstruct a lattice isometry (∑i​ai​xi2​=∑i​ai​yi2​⟹xi2​=yi2​)

Words: 95
Tetracode length-isospectral lattice construction OurBigBook.com
Choose positive axis weights linearly independent over the rationals, and suppose both integer Euclidean lattices contain qZd for some positive integer q. A length-preserving linear map sends each qei​ to an integer vector with exactly that absolute-coordinate pattern, by the displayed implication. Thus the map must be a diagonal sign change. For the four-coordinate tetracode, preserving the code forces all four signs to agree, because each of its four nonzero projective words has support on a different triple of coordinates. A global sign cannot exchange the two odd-vector parity conditions, proving nonisometry for these weights.

Parity congruence description of tetracode lattices (xmod3∈T,x1​≡⋯≡x4​(mod2))

Words: 67
Tetracode length-isospectral lattice construction OurBigBook.com
Add respectively the conditions ∑i​xi​≡0(mod4) and ∑i​xi​−2x1​≡0(mod4) to the displayed common conditions. These define the two integer Euclidean lattices underlying the tetracode length-isospectral lattice construction. They coincide on their all-even vectors and differ on all-odd vectors. Reflecting a coordinate divisible by three preserves the code condition; on odd vectors it changes the coordinate sum by two modulo four, while on even vectors both conditions remain satisfied. This yields the coordinate reflection bijection for tetracode lattices.

Coordinate reflection bijection for tetracode lattices (v↦v−2vi​ei​)

Words: 69
Tetracode length-isospectral lattice construction OurBigBook.com
For the tetracode length-isospectral lattice construction L±​=(±3I+S)Z4, choose the first coordinate i divisible by three and reverse its sign. Such a coordinate always exists because each nonzero tetracode word has one zero coordinate. The reflection preserves the reduction modulo three and switches the two lattice membership conditions modulo four. It is an involution between L+​ and L−​ preserving every absolute coordinate, so arbitrary positive diagonal weights preserve equality of their vector-length multisets.

Covolume (covol(Λ))

Words: 43
Euclidean lattice OurBigBook.com
The covolume of a full Euclidean lattice is the Lebesgue measure of a fundamental parallelepiped in its ambient inner product space. In orthonormal coordinates it is ∣detB∣ for a lattice basis matrix B. Scaling the lattice by t>0 multiplies the covolume by tn; the dual lattice has reciprocal covolume.

Shortest-independent-vector basis lemma

Words: 64
Euclidean lattice OurBigBook.com
In a rank-two Euclidean lattice, a shortest nonzero vector v and a shortest vector w∈/Zv form a basis. The shortest vector is primitive. If the vertical coordinate of w has index m≥2 in the projection lattice, a vector with smaller positive vertical coordinate can be reduced horizontally to length squared at most (∣v∣2+∣w∣2)/4<∣w∣2, a contradiction. This lemma need not hold in higher rank.

The Poisson summation formula equates sample sums of a function and its Fourier transform. Exchanging broad and narrow sums can save work. Use the convention
f​(ξ)=∫R​f(x)e−2πiξxdx.
(9)
For every Schwartz function f∈S(R),
n∈Z∑​f(n)=k∈Z∑​f​(k).​
(10)
Both series have absolute convergence. A sufficient hypothesis is that f is smooth and supx​(1+∣x∣)M∣f(r)(x)∣<∞ for all nonnegative integers M,r; its Fourier transform is then also a Schwartz function.[ref] This assumption controls both decay and regularity; mere membership of an L1 space does not control values at individual sampling points, as periodization of an integrable function illustrates.
Here ξ counts cycles per unit length. In the angular convention used elsewhere in Fourier analysis, f​(ω)=∫f(x)e−iωxdx, so f​(ξ)=f​(2πξ) and the right-hand side becomes ∑k​f​(2πk). At a=1 the Gaussian function is its own Fourier transform; at reciprocal values of a its spatial and spectral widths exchange.

For F∈L1(R) the periodization is absolutely convergent almost everywhere in a period by integrating the sum of absolute values. Wavelet

Words: 4k Articles: 43
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
A wavelet is a localized analyzing function whose shifted and scaled copies examine a signal at different positions and resolutions. Its usefulness is to separate where a change occurs from how large a region that change spans. A brief feature can contribute to a few nearby wavelet coefficients instead of being described entirely through global oscillations.
The Haar wavelet is the simplest example: compare the first half of an interval with the second. A constant value contributes nothing to this contrast, while a difference between the halves survives. Moving the function changes which part of the signal is examined; shrinking it compares smaller neighbouring regions. In an orthonormal wavelet construction, these comparisons fit together without duplicating squared-norm contributions.
A scaling function retains the coarse information that such contrasts omit. The discrete wavelet transform computes both coarse values and details, and the wavelet series recombines them. This gives signal processing a representation that can expose local structure and support image compression. The transform itself is reversible in the complete orthonormal representation; discarding coefficients introduces approximation error. [ref]

Discrete wavelet transform ((a,b)=((u+v)/2​,(u−v)/2​))

Words: 257
Wavelet OurBigBook.com
A discrete wavelet transform computes multiscale approximation and detail coefficients from sampled data. For the Haar wavelet, replace each adjacent pair (u,v) by
a=2​u+v​,d=2​u−v​.
(27)
The approximation coefficient a is 2​ times the pair's arithmetic mean; it is not the ordinary mean. The detail coefficient d records their signed contrast. Repeat on the approximation coefficients until only one remains, keeping every detail coefficient.
For a worked example, start with the vector (2,4,6,8). The first pass gives approximation coefficients (32​,72​) and detail coefficients (−2​,−2​). Transforming the remaining pair gives the coarse coefficient 10 and the half-to-half detail −4. In the order coarse value, coarse detail, then fine details, the transform is
(2,4,6,8)⟼(10,−4,−2​,−2​).​
(28)
This is an orthogonal matrix transformation. Each pair preserves u2+v2=a2+d2, so the full transform preserves the squared Euclidean norm:
22+42+62+82=120=102+(−4)2+(−2​)2+(−2​)2.
(29)
The inverse function for each pair is u=(a+d)/2​, v=(a−d)/2​. Reversing the passes therefore recovers every original value. This squared-norm bookkeeping is often called signal energy; it need not represent physical energy. [ref]
Continuous and discrete normalizations differ. If n=2J data values are interpreted as the heights of a step function on n equal cells of [0,1], its normalized L2 inner product coefficients are the discrete coefficients divided by n​. For our four values they are (5,−2,−1/2​,−1/2​), as the Haar projection example shows. The same normalization is used by the wavelet regression estimator on [0,1].
Under independent Gaussian noise with a common variance, orthogonality preserves that coefficient noise variance and independence. It does not make every arbitrary correlated signal independent: this statistical conclusion uses the Gaussian model and its equal-variance independent inputs.

Wavelet approximation across a curve

Words: 65
Tensor-product wavelet basis OurBigBook.com
A finite-length smooth curve meets O(2j) supports of localized two-dimensional wavelets at scale j. For a bounded function, their coefficients are O(2−j), so their total squared energy at that scale is O(2−j). Keeping these coefficients through level J uses O(2J) terms and leaves squared error O(2−J). Polynomial cancellation, or adequate approximation of the remaining smooth regions, therefore gives best N-term approximation squared error O(N−1).

An interval-adapted wavelet basis is an orthonormal basis of L2[0,1] made of a finite coarse scaling function family and resolution-indexed wavelets. A localized construction modifies only a bounded number of functions near each endpoint at every level. Boundary modification must preserve nested refinement spaces and the required vanishing moments; simple restriction of a whole-line basis does not do so.

Boundary wavelet OurBigBook.com
This construction adapts compactly supported orthonormal wavelets to an interval by finite changes near its endpoints. It preserves local support, polynomial reproduction, nested approximation spaces and orthogonal detail spaces. The resulting basis contains coarse scaling functions, unchanged interior wavelets, and finitely many boundary wavelets per endpoint and per scale, without forcing periodic or zero boundary values.

Vanishing moment (∫xrψ(x)dx=0)

Words: 1k Articles: 6
Wavelet OurBigBook.com
A vanishing moment is a cancellation condition: positive and negative parts of an analyzing function balance when weighted by a monomial. Having q vanishing moments means that the first q such balances hold, starting with the unweighted integral:
∫R​xrψ(x)dx=0,r=0,…,q−1,q≥1.
(30)
Consequently a wavelet ignores local polynomial trends of degree of a polynomial less than q. A smooth feature is close to its Taylor polynomial, so only the small Taylor remainder contributes to its detail coefficient. A jump discontinuity cannot be approximated this way across its edge; its jump response of a localized analyzing function can remain large relative to details from a smooth region.[ref]
These are ordinary absolutely convergent integrals, not a prescription for assigning values to divergent expressions. A sufficient assumption is
∫R​(1+∣x∣q−1)∣ψ(x)∣dx<∞.
(31)
It makes ψ and all xrψ for r<q integrable functions. Being square-integrable alone does not ensure these weighted integrals exist. For a square-integrable function with compact support, the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality guarantees every such weighted integral is finite. Saying exactly q vanishing moments additionally requires an existing, nonzero next integral ∫xqψ(x)dx; the usual phrase “has q” allows more cancellation.

For a>0 and b∈R, define the shifted, scaled analyzing function and its coefficient by
ψa,b​(x)=a−1/2ψ(ax−b​),cψ​(f;a,b)=∫R​f(x)ψa,b​(x)​dx=a​∫R​f(b+au)ψ(u)​du.

Assume the product is integrable; for example this holds for a locally integrable function f and a bounded analyzing function with compact support. The bar is complex conjugation. This normalization preserves the L2 norm of the analyzing function. If p is a polynomial of degree of a polynomial less than q, then p(b+au) is a sum of monomials ur with r<q. Linearity of integration and the vanishing moments give cψ​(p;a,b)=0 at every position and scale. Nonzero polynomials on the whole real line are not square-integrable, so this cancellation is an integral pairing; it is not a claim that these polynomials are vectors of L2(R).
Here is a quantitative reason that smooth regions yield small details. Let ψ have compact support and q vanishing moments, and suppose f is q times continuously differentiable on an interval containing b and b+asuppψ. Subtract its degree-(q−1) Taylor polynomial at b. If ∣f(q)∣≤M on that interval, the Taylor remainder bound gives

Thus the analyzing function measures the departure from the local polynomial trend, rather than the height of f itself. The wavelet coefficient decay for Hölder functions uses the same argument with a Hölder-Taylor remainder bound. These estimates concern regularity of f on the analyzing function's entire support of a function; extra vanishing moments alone do not make ψ smooth or establish an orthonormal wavelet construction.[ref]

Orthonormal wavelet (ψj,k​(x)=2j/2ψ(2jx−k))

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Wavelet OurBigBook.com
An orthonormal wavelet ψ generates an orthonormal basis of L2(R) through
ψj,k​(x)=2j/2ψ(2jx−k),j,k∈Z.
(44)
The factor 2j/2 compensates for the shrinking support of a function, keeping the L2 norm equal to one. Orthogonality makes different coefficients separate squared-norm contributions, and completeness allows the wavelet series to recover any square-integrable function in the L2 norm.
For the Haar wavelet, wavelets at one scale have disjoint supports. At different scales their dyadic intervals are either disjoint or nested. On the support of the finer wavelet, the coarser one is constant, while the finer one has zero integral, so their L2 inner product is zero. Together with the unit L2 norm, this explains orthonormality. On the bounded interval [0,1], add the constant Haar scaling function and use j≥0, 0≤k<2j; the constant function is not an L2(R) basis element on the whole line.

A Daubechies wavelet of order q is a compact support orthonormal wavelet with q vanishing moments and a minimal-length finite refinement filter. The minimal filter has 2q taps, giving support length 2q−1 in the standard dyadic normalization. Its low-pass symbol has a zero of order q at π. Increasing order improves polynomial cancellation and, for sufficiently large order, regularity, at the price of a wider support.

Orthonormal wavelet OurBigBook.com
The Haar wavelet is a signed contrast between two adjacent half-intervals:
ψ(x)=⎩⎨⎧​1,−1,0,​0≤x<1/2,1/2≤x<1,otherwise.​
(45)
It has compact support, zero integral, and unit L2 norm: ∫ψ=1/2−1/2=0 and ∫∣ψ∣2=1. The zero integral is its one vanishing moment. Its Haar scaling function is ϕ=1[0,1)​, which records a coarse value rather than a contrast. Endpoint conventions do not alter the L2 inner products.
The normalized copies ψj,k​(x)=2j/2ψ(2jx−k) compare the halves of the dyadic interval [k2−j,(k+1)2−j). Narrower copies are taller so that their L2 norms stay one. Thus a coefficient identifies both a location, through k, and a scale, through j.
For a simple step function f equal to 2 on [0,1/2) and 6 on [1/2,1), its coarse coefficient is ⟨f,ϕ⟩=4, while its first contrast is ⟨f,ψ⟩=−2. Thus f=4ϕ−2ψ. The negative coefficient raises the second half and lowers the first. Finer contrasts vanish because f is constant on each half. A jump aligned with this dyadic interval boundary therefore needs only two nonzero coefficients; jumps at other positions can require details at many scales.
Its jump discontinuities make the Haar wavelet particularly transparent for changes between neighbouring regions, while limiting approximation of smooth variation. A Daubechies wavelet uses a more elaborate pattern to obtain additional vanishing moments and, at sufficiently high order, smoother basis functions. The elementary Haar refinement identity has coefficients h0​=h1​=1/2​ and explains how the coarse and fine descriptions fit together.
The historical source is Alfred Haar's [ref]. Chapter III, beginning on page 361, constructs the constant function and these localized piecewise-constant orthogonal functions. Its original endpoint assignments differ from the half-open convention used here, without changing L2 inner products.

The Haar projection at level J is the orthogonal projection onto the functions constant on level-J dyadic intervals. On each cell it replaces f by its cell average. This is the closest cellwise-constant approximation in the L2 norm, because choosing a constant c on a cell minimizes ∫I​∣f−c∣2 at its cell average.
On [0,1], take the step function with values 2,4,6,8 on successive quarter-intervals. At level zero, its Haar projection is the constant 5. At level one, it has values 3 and 7 on the two halves. At level two, it recovers the four original values exactly. With normalized Haar wavelets, these approximations are
P0​f=5ϕ,P1​f=5ϕ−2ψ,P2​f=5ϕ−2ψ−2​1​ψ1,0​−2​1​ψ1,1​.

The approximation errors in squared L2 norm of P0​f,P1​f,P2​f are respectively 5,1,0: each added detail removes exactly its own squared coefficient from the error.

On [0,1] with lowest level zero, that coarse family is the single constant function ϕ. Multiresolution analysis

Words: 1k Articles: 15
Wavelet OurBigBook.com
A multiresolution analysis organizes a function into successively finer approximation spaces. In the usual orthonormal construction on L2(R), these are closed linear subspaces (Vj​)j∈Z​ with
Vj​⊆Vj+1​,⋃j​Vj​​=L2(R),⋂j​Vj​={0}.
(51)
Rescaling relates the levels: f(x)∈Vj​ if and only if f(2x)∈Vj+1​. Integer translates of a scaling function form an orthonormal basis of V0​. The detail space is the orthogonal complement of Vj​ inside Vj+1​, giving Vj+1​=Vj​⊕Wj​. Coarse information and new details therefore fit together without overlap in squared L2 norm.
For the Haar wavelet, Vj​ consists of square-integrable functions constant on cells of length 2−j. Splitting every cell into two halves creates one new contrast per old cell, the Haar refinement identity. On the bounded example [0,1], the first three spaces have dimensions 1,2,4: a whole-interval mean, two half-interval means, and four quarter-interval means. The Haar projection diagram displays those three resolutions. This bounded construction starts at level zero; the displayed intersection condition refers to the full family on the real line.
The usefulness is a controlled way to increase resolution. Earlier coarse information remains available while new wavelet coefficients identify what the finer description adds. The wavelet approximation complexity connects this extra resolution to both approximation error and the number of coefficients being estimated. [ref]

A Fourier mode is a single complex oscillatory component eiωx. Its real and imaginary parts are a cosine and a sine; ω is the spatial angular frequency. Every constant-coefficient differential operator acts on it by multiplication: P(∂x​)eiωx=P(iω)eiωx. In particular, ∂x2​eiωx=−ω2eiωx. These eigenfunctions reduce a partial differential equation such as the heat equation to separate equations for each frequency. On the real line a pure Fourier mode is not in the L2 space; the Fourier transform uses such modes in a continuous superposition.

Fourier inversion theorem (F−1)

Words: 499 Articles: 4
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
The Fourier inversion theorem makes decomposition into frequencies reversible: a complete Fourier transform, including its wave phases, determines the original function up to equality almost everywhere. With the angular-frequency convention
f​(ξ)=∫Rn​e−ix⋅ξf(x)dx,
(62)
if f and f​ belong to the L1 space, then
f(x)=(2π)n1​∫Rn​eix⋅ξf​(ξ)dξ
(63)
almost everywhere. The right side is a continuous representative of f. If f itself is continuous, equality holds everywhere, as explained by the continuous version of Fourier inversion. The integrability hypotheses ensure that both displayed integrals are ordinary absolutely convergent integrals. For arbitrary elements of the L2 space, the Plancherel theorem instead supplies inversion in the L2 space norm.
Each factor eix⋅ξ is a Fourier mode; the inverse integral adds them with the complex weights f​(ξ)/(2π)n. The normalization is part of the recipe. In one dimension, writing ordinary frequency as ν=ξ/(2π) gives the equivalent pair
F(ν)=∫R​f(t)e−2πiνtdt,f(t)=∫R​F(ν)e2πiνtdν,
(64)
where F(ν)=f​(2πν). Reversing both exponential signs gives another equivalent convention, but the forward and inverse formulas must use opposite signs consistently.
For example, the Fourier transform of a Gaussian gives
f(x)=e−ax2,f​(ξ)=aπ​​e−ξ2/(4a),a>0.
(65)
Fourier inversion says that a weighted continuum of oscillations reconstructs this smooth Gaussian function. Narrowing the original Gaussian function by increasing a broadens its frequency spectrum. This is a concrete demonstration that a sharply localized shape needs a wider range of frequencies.
Inversion is what makes a frequency calculation useful: transform a function, solve the simpler problem there, then return to the original variables. A brief proof outline is to multiply f​(ξ) by e−ϵ∣ξ∣2, ϵ>0. The inverse integral becomes convolution with a normalized Gaussian function, an approximate identity. As ϵ tends to zero, dominated convergence gives the unregularized inverse integral, while the approximate identity recovers f almost everywhere. Joseph Fourier's Théorie analytique de la chaleur (1822), Chapter IX, article 417, contains a cosine double-integral representation antecedent to this modern formula; the hypotheses above are the modern statement.[ref]

Convolution ((f∗g)(x)=∫R​f(y)g(x−y)dy)

Words: 3k Articles: 36
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
Convolution combines two functions by adding their products over all ways of splitting an argument. For Lebesgue integrable functions f,g on the real line, their convolution is
(f∗g)(x)=∫R​f(y)g(x−y)dy.
(71)
The arguments y and x−y always add to x. For f,g in the L1 space, the integral exists almost everywhere and defines another element of the L1 space, with ∥f∗g∥1​≤∥f∥1​∥g∥1​ by Young's convolution inequality. Particular examples below have a value at every x.
To see what the integral counts, take the indicator function q=1[0,1]​. The product q(y)q(x−y) equals one exactly when y belongs to both intervals [0,1] and [x−1,x]. Its integral is their overlap length, so
(q∗q)(x)=⎩⎨⎧​x,2−x,0,​0≤x≤1,1<x≤2,otherwise.​
(72)
At x=1/2, the overlap is [0,1/2] and the output is 1/2; at x=1, the two intervals coincide and the output is one. The result is the shifted triangular function tri(x−1). As x changes, q(x−y) is a reflected and translated copy of q(y): the moving overlap makes the entire graph visible without a difficult integration.
The same calculation gives the probability distribution of a sum of two independent random variables. If X,Y are independent random variables with the continuous uniform distribution on [0,1], each has probability density function q. Their sum has probability density function q∗q by convolution of probability densities. The probability density function at one is larger than near zero or two because there are more combinations of the two inputs giving that sum. Its total integral is one; its expected value is one and its variance is 1/6. These follow equally from integrating the triangular function or from linearity of expectation and variance additivity for independent random variables.
Convolution also gives a useful averaging operation. For ε>0, let kε​(y)=1[−ε,ε]​(y)/(2ε). Then
(f∗kε​)(x)=2ε1​∫x−εx+ε​f(u)du,
(73)
the mean of f in a neighborhood of x. A smaller ε examines a smaller neighborhood. For a continuous function f, this mean tends to f(x) as ε→0, an example of an approximate identity. Integrating a sharp input against a distributed convolution kernel can produce a smoother output; the triangular example turns two discontinuous inputs into a continuous output.
In signal processing, a linear time-invariant system combines shifted copies of its impulse response by the same rule. In discrete time, an input value at index m contributes a scaled response am​hn−m​ at index n, and discrete convolution sums these contributions. This is the superposition interpretation developed in Oppenheim, MIT Signals and Systems, Lecture 4, convolution sums and integrals. The convolution theorem then gives another description: transform both inputs with a Fourier transform and multiply their transforms. Combining shifts, combining independent quantities and multiplying frequency descriptions are three faces of the same operation.

A term am​zm times bk​zk contributes to coefficient m+k, precisely the index condition in discrete convolution. In probability, a counts the outcomes of two independent fair coin tosses by their number of heads, while b counts the outcomes of one more toss. Dividing the output by eight gives the probability mass function (1,3,3,1)/8 of the binomial distribution with n=3 and p=1/2. No new arithmetic is needed to pass from coefficient multiplication to counting independent sums.
The full finite convolution is different from circular convolution, where indices wrap modulo a chosen length. Wrapping this four-term output to length three adds its last entry to its first and gives (2,3,3). When using a discrete Fourier transform to compute the full convolution, zero padding to length at least the sum of the input lengths minus one prevents this wraparound. [ref]

For a proof outline, Fubini's theorem permits exchanging the two integrals because the integral of ∣f(y)g(x−y)∣ over (x,y) is ∥f∥1​∥g∥1​<∞. Set u=x−y in the inner integral:

(88)
The factorization of the complex exponential is the mechanism behind the simplification. The discrete convolution version similarly turns coefficient sums into products of generating functions.

With Fourier transform convention f​(k)=∫f(x)e−ikxdx, one has f​(k)=2a/(a2+k2). The convolution theorem and Fourier inversion theorem therefore yield
∫R​(a2+k2)2eikx​dk=2a3π​(1+a∣x∣)e−a∣x∣.​

The displayed unbounded limsup follows, although every individual continuous function still has coefficients tending to zero by the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma.

Riemann-Lebesgue lemma OurBigBook.com
For a continuous real function f on [a,b], uniform step approximation on a compact interval gives a finite step function g=∑j​cj​1Ij​​ with small uniform error. Each cosine integral over an interval has absolute value at most 2/∣ω∣. Therefore
​∫ab​f(t)cos(ωt)dt​≤(b−a)∥f−g∥∞​+∣ω∣2​∑j​∣cj​∣.

First choose g to make the first term small, then let ∣ω∣ grow with g fixed. This proves the cosine version of the Riemann-Lebesgue lemma without differentiating f; the sine and complex-exponential versions follow in the same way.

Fourier restriction theory

Words: 1k Articles: 22
Fourier analysis OurBigBook.com
Fourier restriction theory studies estimates for Fourier transforms restricted to curved submanifolds and for the corresponding extension operators.

Discrete paraboloid (P={(v,v⋅v):v∈Fpd−1​})

Words: 219 Articles: 2
Fourier restriction theory OurBigBook.com
The discrete paraboloid is the graph of the sum-of-squares quadratic form in a vector space over a finite field. Its surface measure is normalized counting measure, of total mass one. A Fourier extension operator takes a function on this graph to its character sum in the ambient finite vector space. Ambient counting measure and normalized surface measure must be distinguished when defining a restriction constant.

Isotropic-line obstruction to finite-field restriction (R∗(2→q)≥p2/q−1/2)

Words: 54
Discrete paraboloid OurBigBook.com
If i2=−1 in the prime field, the line ℓ={(t,it,0):t∈Fp​} lies in the three-dimensional discrete paraboloid. Its indicator has normalized surface L2 norm p−1/2. Its extension is p−1 on the two-dimensional annihilator plane and zero elsewhere. Thus its ambient ℓq norm is p2/q−1, proving the displayed lower bound, which diverges for q<4.

Finite-field paraboloid fourth-moment extension estimate (R∗(2→4)≤2​)

Words: 105
Discrete paraboloid OurBigBook.com
For the three-dimensional discrete paraboloid over an odd prime field, the surface transform away from zero has magnitude at most p−1, by completing squares and evaluating Quadratic Gauss sums. The adjoint-composition convolution kernel is the transform of the surface measure. Subtract its unit mass at the origin. Convolution by the remainder has ℓ1→ℓ∞ norm at most p−1 and ℓ2→ℓ2 norm at most p. The Riesz-Thorin interpolation theorem gives ℓ4/3→ℓ4 norm at most one; adding the identity kernel gives at most two. The adjoint-composition identity and duality therefore give the displayed extension constant for normalized surface measure and ambient counting measure. This argument works for either quadratic character of minus one.

Restriction-to-rectangle overlap principle (∫(∑R​1R​)p/2≲p​δ4−p∑R​∣R∣)

Words: 76
Fourier restriction theory OurBigBook.com
Assume a finite diagonal Fourier extension estimate on the unit circle. For direction-separated rectangles of dimensions δ−2×δ−1, choose disjoint frequency caps and translate their transforms to the rectangles by the Fourier modulation and translation identity. Randomize their signs. Disjointness gives an input pth-power norm at most CMδ; the Khintchine inequality converts the averaged output norm into the square function. The circle cap Fourier lower bound gives δp∫(∑R​1R​)p/2≲p​Mδ. Each rectangle has area δ−3, giving the displayed form. Input cap disjointness is compatible with arbitrary spatial rectangle overlap.

Words: 343 Articles: 4
Fourier restriction theory OurBigBook.com
A Fourier extension operator forms an oscillatory integral from a density on a frequency surface with measure σ. The opposite sign in the phase merely reflects the output variable, so it gives identical Lp norms. In the usual dual formulation it is the adjoint of restricting the Fourier transform to that surface.

Words: 73
Fourier extension operator OurBigBook.com
Let μ be a finite positive surface measure and ∣f∣≤1. Expand ∣fμ​(x)∣2k and integrate against e−π∣x∣2/R2. The Fourier transform of a Gaussian turns the oscillatory kernel into Rde−πR2∣∑j≤k​ωj​−∑j>k​ωj​∣2, which is nonnegative. Taking absolute values of the bounded amplitudes gives an upper bound by the same moment with f=1. This weighted positivity is valid even when f is merely measurable; it transfers a scalar surface-decay estimate to a local bounded-density moment estimate.

For normalized circle measure and a nonnegative cutoff near (1,0), equal to one on ∣θ∣≤δ/C and supported on ∣θ∣≤2δ/C, remove the constant phase e−iξ1​. On ∣ξ1​∣≤δ−2, ∣ξ2​∣≤δ−1, the remaining phase has magnitude at most 2/C2+2/C. Taking C sufficiently large keeps its real part positive and comparable to one, so the Fourier transform has magnitude at least a constant times the cap mass, which is at least δ/(πC). No upper bound on the cutoff is required for this lower bound.

An extension estimate is a norm bound for the Fourier extension operator, uniform over its input. The exponents encode the curvature and scale of the frequency surface. For normalized circle measure, a cap of angular width δ produces size comparable to δ on a rectangle of dimensions δ−2×δ−1. This single-cap example forces p≥4 for a finite diagonal estimate with the same exponent p on both sides.

Fourier extension estimate OurBigBook.com
On the unit circle, the arclength-measure transform satisfies ∣σ(x)∣≲(1+∣x∣)−1/2. This follows by removing angular neighborhoods of width ∣x∣−1/2 around the two stationary points and integrating by parts on the remainder. Gaussian positivity for even extension moments bounds the weighted fourth moment for any bounded f by that for f=1. Radial integration of (1+r)−2e−πr2/R2 with area element rdr costs only logR, proving the displayed local estimate. Modulated disjoint caps and random signs convert it into the planar Kakeya neighborhood lower bound.

For a direction e, the Kakeya maximal function is the supremum over translations of normalized averages of ∣f∣ over unit-length Kakeya tubes in direction e. It measures how large a function can be on at least one thin tube in each direction. Normalizing by tube volume is essential when comparing different thicknesses.

Constants may depend on dimension and ε, but not tube thickness or the function. Applied to an indicator function of a neighborhood of a Kakeya set, it gives the Kakeya Minkowski dimension conjecture.

For a separated angular net, two translated unit rectangles of width δ intersect in area at most a constant times δ2/(δ+α), where α is their unoriented angular distance. Each row of their intersection matrix therefore has sum at most Cδlog(2/δ). Applying the Schur test to the adjoint averaging operator gives the displayed bound. A wider-tube comparison extends it from the net to all directions. Since log(2/δ)​≲ε​δ−ε, this proves the planar version of the Kakeya maximal conjecture.
